cases.case_name: Kent K. v. Bobby M.
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court held that while a statutory ground for termination must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, the best-interests determination need only be proved by a preponderance of the evidence, and it vacated the contrary portion of the court of appeals' decision.
cases.quote: we hold today that preponderance of the evidence, rather than clear and convincing evidence, is the proper standard of proof to be applied to the best interests inquiry

relevance.OUT-02: This is the controlling Arizona case fixing the two-tier burden of proof at termination — clear and convincing for the statutory ground, preponderance for best interests.

cases.case_name: Alma S. v. Dep't of Child Safety
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the severance order, holding that the best-interests inquiry is a totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry that includes the child's adoptability and the parent's rehabilitation but may not subordinate the child's interests to the parent's once a ground is proved.
cases.quote: We hold that courts must consider the totality of the circumstances existing at the time of the severance determination, including the child's adoptability and the parent's rehabilitation.

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the substantive content of the best-interests finding that Kent K. leaves at the preponderance standard.
relevance.FAIL-01: Illustrates the limits on appellate reversal of a juvenile court's best-interests finding — the reviewing court may not reweigh the evidence or elevate parental interests.

cases.case_name: Michael J. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's rights on the abandonment ground, holding that the statutory abandonment definition applies to married and unmarried parents alike and that incarceration is one factor in, but not a defense to, the abandonment analysis.
cases.quote: His incarceration alone, however, does not justify a failure to make more than minimal efforts to support and communicate with his child.

relevance.OUT-02: Leading Arizona authority on abandonment and on how an incarcerated parent's conduct is measured, and the source of the six-factor length-of-sentence test.

cases.case_name: Brenda D. v. Dep't of Child Safety
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court affirmed the termination order, holding that a parent who arrives late to a duly noticed termination adjudication has 'failed to appear,' but that the absent parent's counsel retains the right to participate fully and the State must still prove a ground and best interests.
cases.quote: we hold that a parent who fails to timely appear for a scheduled and duly-noticed termination adjudication hearing has "failed to appear" under § 8-863(C) and Rule 66(D)(2)

relevance.FAIL-01: Defines when a procedural default at a termination hearing does — and does not — justify reversal, and confirms the State's burden survives a parent's non-appearance.

cases.case_name: Valerie M. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court held that ICWA does not require Arizona's state-law termination grounds or the best-interests finding to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt; that standard under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(f) governs only the finding that continued custody is likely to cause serious emotional or physical damage.
cases.quote: We do not believe that Congress intended to apply the reasonable doubt standard to state-law findings.

relevance.INP-11: Controlling Arizona authority on how ICWA's heightened proof requirement interacts with state-law findings once a case is identified as involving an Indian child.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of Parental Rights as to B.W.
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court reversed and remanded, defining 'just cause' under the abandonment ground as a reasonable and fair justification for not maintaining a normal parental relationship on which the parent relied in good faith.
cases.quote: parents have "just cause" when they had a reasonable and fair justification for not maintaining a normal parental relationship with the child and relied on that justification in good faith

relevance.OUT-02: Current Arizona Supreme Court gloss on the 'just cause' defense to the abandonment ground for termination.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of Parental Rights as to M.N.
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court reversed and remanded, holding that a man identified as a potential father and served with notice under A.R.S. § 8-106(G) is not required to file with the putative fathers registry and so cannot have his rights terminated under § 8-533(B)(6) for failing to do so.
cases.quote: a potential father's rights cannot be terminated under § 8-533(B)(6) for noncompliance with § 8-106.01

relevance.DEC-05: Governs who must be served and what notice-based grounds may be pleaded when the agency or a private party opens a case affecting an alleged father's rights.

cases.case_name: Jessie D. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's rights, holding that although the juvenile court misapplied a Michael J. factor, DCS owes incarcerated parents a diligent effort to preserve the family and reasonable evidence supported the best-interests finding.
cases.quote: DCS must make diligent efforts to preserve the family by providing services to assist parents in maintaining a bond with their children

relevance.ACT-01: States the agency's affirmative service obligation that underlies any voluntary service plan offered short of court compulsion.
relevance.ACT-02: Confirms that court-ordered service plans must actually be supported by DCS's diligent efforts, including for incarcerated parents.
relevance.OUT-01: Diligent agency effort is the precondition to treating reunification as unachievable.

cases.case_name: Timothy B. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court reversed and remanded, holding that a 'normal home' under the length-of-sentence ground does not require the incarcerated parent's physical presence and adding the availability of a permanent guardian to the Michael J. factors.
cases.quote: We modify the fifth factor by adding that the court should consider the availability of a permanent guardian to provide a normal home life if another parent is unavailable.

relevance.ACT-04: Makes a relative or kin caregiver's willingness to serve as permanent guardian a factor the court must weigh before severing an incarcerated parent's rights.
relevance.OUT-03: Establishes permanent guardianship as a live alternative to termination that the juvenile court must consider on the record.

cases.case_name: Brionna J. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the termination order, holding that the intermediate court misapplied the fifteen-months-in-care ground, reweighed the evidence, used the wrong standard of review, and could not dismiss the dependency in an appeal from the termination order.
cases.quote: The court of appeals also erred when it exceeded the proper scope of review by reweighing the evidence presented to the juvenile court.

relevance.ACT-02: Restates the three elements of the fifteen-month ground, including DCS's diligent effort to provide appropriate reunification services.
relevance.OUT-01: Sets the evidentiary frame for deciding when reunification has ceased to be achievable after fifteen months in care.
relevance.OUT-05: Confirms that a dependency finding cannot be collaterally dismissed through an appeal of the later termination order.
relevance.FAIL-01: The leading recent statement of the limits on appellate reversal of juvenile court decisions in Arizona.

cases.case_name: Silverman v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court held that investigative journalists can qualify as persons conducting 'bona fide research' under the confidentiality statute's exception, vacated the court of appeals' opinion, and remanded for the agency to exercise its release discretion under the definition the Court supplied.
cases.quote: The primary issue before us is whether investigative journalists can engage in "bona fide research." We conclude they can.

relevance.INP-09: Shows how outside researchers and journalists can lawfully obtain protective-services records that seed oversight inquiries.
relevance.FAIL-06: Establishes that a blanket confidentiality statute does not let a protective-services agency refuse all outside inspection.
relevance.PMC-02: Supports access to agency records needed to test audit and financial findings.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports the record access that independent review bodies depend on.
relevance.PMC-04: Supports outside access to case records underlying fatality and serious-injury reviews.
relevance.PMC-05: Arizona's most recent supreme court construction of a protective-services records exception favoring disclosure.
relevance.PMC-06: Confirms that systematic analysis of agency records can constitute 'bona fide research' entitled to statutory access.

cases.case_name: Griffis v. Pinal County
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court held that purely personal documents of a public officer are not public records but that the custodian's assertion is not conclusive, reversed the superior court, vacated the court of appeals' opinion, and remanded for in camera inspection.
cases.quote: Arizona law defines "public records" broadly and creates a presumption requiring the disclosure of public documents

relevance.INP-09: Supplies the presumption of disclosure that oversight bodies and the public rely on to obtain agency records.
relevance.FAIL-06: The controlling Arizona statement that non-disclosure is the exception and must be justified record by record.
relevance.PMC-01: Anchors public access to the performance data underlying federal monitoring.
relevance.PMC-02: Anchors public access to audit and financial records held by state agencies.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports the record access that citizen review panels require to function.
relevance.PMC-05: Arizona's leading public-records decision, including the availability of in camera judicial review of withheld documents.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes that the burden of justifying withholding rests on the agency, not the requester.

cases.case_name: Mary Ellen C. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals reversed the severance order because the State failed to make reasonable efforts to preserve the family, holding that the duty to provide rehabilitative services with a reasonable possibility of success has a constitutional basis.
cases.quote: although the State is not obliged to undertake futile rehabilitative measures, it is obliged to undertake those which offer a reasonable possibility of success

relevance.INP-05: Frames the State's obligation to respond to a family that seeks or needs help with services that could actually work.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports resolving a case through meaningful services rather than a petition where services offer a reasonable possibility of success.
relevance.ACT-01: The foundational Arizona statement of what an adequate service plan must look like.
relevance.ACT-02: Establishes that court-ordered services must be timely and tailored, not nominal.
relevance.OUT-01: Reversal for failure to make reasonable efforts is the principal check protecting the reunification goal.

cases.case_name: American Civil Liberties Union of Arizona v. Arizona Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The court of appeals held that the electronic records and data DCS maintains in its CHILDS case-management system are public records subject to Arizona's public records law, affirming in part, reversing in part, and remanding.
cases.quote: Under any of the formulations of a public record discussed above, and based on its content, CHILDS is a public record.

relevance.INP-09: Makes the agency's own case-management data reachable by outside oversight and audit requests.
relevance.OUT-06: Provides the mechanism for obtaining the agency records that document fatalities and serious injuries in care.
relevance.FAIL-03: Gives the public a route to the state performance data that federal compliance review depends on.
relevance.FAIL-04: Establishes that DCS cannot treat its electronic child-death and supervision records as categorically beyond disclosure.
relevance.FAIL-06: The controlling Arizona decision on a child-welfare agency's obligation to disclose its records.
relevance.PMC-01: Opens the state data on safety and permanency outcomes that CFSR monitoring measures.
relevance.PMC-02: Opens the agency records needed to verify audit and grant-expenditure findings.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports citizen review panels' access to the agency's own case data.
relevance.PMC-04: Supports fatality review access to DCS's electronic case records.
relevance.PMC-05: The Arizona case directly holding a child-welfare database to be a disclosable public record.
relevance.PMC-06: Legitimizes systematic, database-level analysis of DCS records as a public-records use.

cases.case_name: Ramsey v. Yavapai Family Advocacy Center
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed summary judgment for the reporter and the forensic interviewers, holding that A.R.S. § 13-3620(J) confers qualified immunity conditioned on the initial reporter's reasonable belief that abuse occurred and that a counselor owes no duty to a third-party alleged abuser.
cases.quote: as the initial reporter of the alleged abuse, Sheets enjoys qualified immunity under the statute only if she "reasonably believe[d]" abuse had occurred

relevance.INP-01: States the exact condition — reasonable belief — on which a mandatory reporter's statutory immunity turns.
relevance.INP-02: Applies the same statutory immunity analysis to any person who reports suspected abuse.
relevance.INP-06: Confirms that immunity protects the hotline report itself only where the reporter reasonably believed abuse occurred.
relevance.INP-07: Extends immunity to healthcare and advocacy-center personnel who participate in the resulting investigation.
relevance.DEC-01: Bears on liability exposure when a report is later unfounded or screened out.
relevance.DEC-03: Clarifies that those who participate in the resulting investigation are immune independent of the reasonable-belief condition placed on the initial reporter.

cases.case_name: L.A.R. v. Ludwig
cases.holding: The court of appeals held that a person with reasonable grounds to report suspected child abuse has qualified statutory immunity defeasible only by proof of malice, but reversed and remanded because the immunity ruling did not dispose of the plaintiffs' separate negligent-treatment and consortium claims.
cases.quote: Malicious intent must be proved by the plaintiff to defeat the defense of qualified immunity.

relevance.INP-01: Places the burden of proving malice on anyone suing a mandatory reporter, and confirms 'reasonable grounds' is a low threshold.
relevance.INP-02: Governs civil exposure of any voluntary reporter of suspected abuse.
relevance.INP-06: Protects good-faith hotline reports absent proof of malice.
relevance.INP-08: Applies the reasonable-grounds immunity standard to school counselors and similar professionals who report.
relevance.DEC-01: Shows that an ultimately unfounded report does not by itself expose the reporter to liability.

cases.case_name: Gila River Indian Community v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the denial of the tribe's transfer motion, holding that 25 U.S.C. § 1911(b) permits transfer only of foster-care-placement and termination proceedings, not of preadoptive or adoptive placement proceedings occurring after parental rights are terminated.
cases.quote: under § 1911(b), ICWA provides only for transfer of state juvenile court proceedings before termination of parental rights, and not for post-termination preadoptive and adoptive placements

relevance.INP-11: Fixes the deadline for invoking tribal jurisdiction in an Arizona ICWA case — transfer must be sought before parental rights are terminated.

cases.case_name: Navajo Nation v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the juvenile court's good-cause finding to deviate from ICWA's placement preferences, holding that the child's bonding with the current placement and the risk of severe emotional harm from removal are permissible good-cause factors when weighed against the tribe's interest.
cases.quote: we have previously held that bonding and the risk of emotional harm are relevant factors in finding good cause to deviate from ICWA placement preferences

relevance.INP-11: Defines how Arizona courts apply ICWA's placement preferences and the 'good cause' escape from them.
relevance.ACT-04: Governs when an agency may place an Indian child outside the statutory relative and tribal preference order.
relevance.FAIL-05: Marks the boundary between a lawful, individualized good-cause deviation and an impermissible disregard of a child's tribal heritage.

cases.case_name: Jeff D. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed an order changing the child's placement from long-term foster parents to a great-aunt and uncle, holding that foster parents' due-process rights are not equivalent to birth parents' and that the court properly weighed the statutory kinship preference against the risk of another move.
cases.quote: We hold the superior court did not violate the foster family's due-process rights and did not abuse its discretion by granting the change.

relevance.ACT-03: Defines the limited procedural rights foster parents hold when a court changes a child's foster placement.
relevance.ACT-04: The leading Arizona construction of the A.R.S. § 8-514(B) placement preferences, including the kinship category.

cases.case_name: Dep't of Child Safety v. Stocking-Tate
cases.holding: The court of appeals granted special action relief and vacated the order striking the ex parte temporary custody order, holding that an ex parte removal order is not challenged by a motion to strike but is reviewed at the statutory temporary custody hearing, where DCS bears the probable-cause burden.
cases.quote: DCS bears the burden of proving "there is probable cause to believe that continued temporary custody of the child is clearly necessary to prevent abuse or neglect."

relevance.INP-04: Describes the ex parte judicial authorization process that precedes or accompanies a court-triggered custody action.
relevance.INP-10: Shows how an investigation escalates into court-authorized temporary custody and the 72-hour limit on that authority.
relevance.INP-12: The controlling Arizona case on the procedure and burden governing emergency protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Fixes what DCS must prove, and when, after an emergency removal decision.
relevance.DEC-05: Explains that the ex parte order expires unless a dependency petition is filed within 72 hours.
relevance.ACT-03: Sets the recurring judicial review of continued out-of-home placement at the dependency, disposition, and review hearings.
relevance.ACT-05: Identifies the temporary orders a juvenile court may issue for the child's safety on the filing of a petition.

cases.case_name: Louis C. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the dependency adjudication, holding that A.R.S. § 8-844(C) requires the juvenile court to adjudicate dependency on a preponderance of the evidence and that the Parents' Bill of Rights does not raise that burden.
cases.quote: Section 8-844(C) not only permits a court to enter an order of dependency based on a preponderance of the evidence, but directs that a court "shall" do so.

relevance.INP-04: Sets the standard the juvenile court applies once a referral results in a dependency proceeding.
relevance.INP-10: Identifies the evidentiary threshold an escalated investigation must ultimately meet in court.
relevance.DEC-03: Confirms that an agency finding of abuse or neglect must be independently proved to the court by a preponderance.
relevance.DEC-05: The controlling Arizona statement of the burden of proof at dependency adjudication.
relevance.ACT-05: Supplies the factual predicate — abuse or need for effective parental care — on which protective orders in a dependency rest.
relevance.OUT-05: A case must be dismissed where the agency cannot carry even the preponderance burden.

cases.case_name: Oscar F. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the dependency adjudication, holding the juvenile court had statutory authority to find the children dependent as to one parent notwithstanding the petition's allegations or the failure to serve the other parent or guardian.
cases.quote: The juvenile court was authorized by statute to adjudicate the children dependent as to Oscar, notwithstanding allegations in the petition or that another parent or guardian has not been served.

relevance.INP-04: Confirms the juvenile court's authority to proceed against one parent when a referral reaches the court.
relevance.DEC-03: Shows that a dependency finding may rest on the statutory definitions of neglect and unfitness rather than on the petition's precise framing.
relevance.DEC-05: Governs the pleading and service defects that do not defeat a dependency petition.

cases.case_name: Donald W. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the severance order as to the father, holding that parents have a right to effective assistance of appointed counsel in severance proceedings grounded in the severance statute and due process, measured by a fundamental-fairness inquiry rather than Strickland's Sixth Amendment test.
cases.quote: the right to effective assistance of counsel in termination proceedings stems from Arizona's juvenile severance statute and the Due Process Clause, not the Sixth Amendment

relevance.FAIL-01: The controlling Arizona standard for reversing a termination order on ineffective-assistance grounds.

cases.case_name: Shawanee S. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the termination order, holding that although the agency must prove a diligent effort to provide appropriate reunification services on a length-of-time-in-care ground, a parent who never objects in the juvenile court waives an appellate challenge to that finding.
cases.quote: when ADES seeks severance based on length of time in care, ADES must prove that it "has made a diligent effort to provide appropriate reunification services."

relevance.INP-05: Establishes that a parent must raise service inadequacy in the juvenile court to preserve it.
relevance.DEC-06: Confirms the agency's service obligation exists independently of whether the case proceeds by petition.
relevance.ACT-01: Shows that a parent must contest the adequacy of offered services contemporaneously, not later.
relevance.ACT-02: States the diligent-effort element the agency must prove when it relies on time in out-of-home care.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines the service record against which a failed reunification is measured.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of C.M.
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the denial of the child's own motion for permanent guardianship, holding that the party seeking permanent guardianship bears the burden of proving the statutory criteria by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: The party seeking a permanent guardianship bears the burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-03: States who bears the burden and to what standard when permanency is sought through guardianship rather than adoption.
relevance.OUT-04: Applies to an older youth's own effort to secure a permanent legal arrangement as she approaches majority.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of A.K.
cases.holding: The court of appeals held that the superior court violated the petitioners' due process rights by deciding the ICWA jurisdictional question without briefing, and that although a guardianship petition is not a foster-care, termination, or adoptive placement proceeding under § 1911, it is a preadoptive placement to which ICWA's placement preferences apply on remand.
cases.quote: This interpretation allows the superior court on remand to exercise jurisdiction to adjudicate the Danforths' guardianship petition but requires the court to consider ICWA's placement preferences.

relevance.INP-11: Determines which guardianship proceedings trigger tribal jurisdiction and which merely trigger ICWA's placement preferences.
relevance.OUT-03: Controls how ICWA constrains an Arizona court's choice of guardian for an Indian child.

cases.case_name: Tammy M. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The court of appeals reversed the termination order and remanded because the juvenile court abused its discretion in denying the mother's request, and held it lacked appellate jurisdiction over the earlier removal-approval order, which was itself final and appealable within fifteen days.
cases.quote: To the extent Tammy challenges it, we lack jurisdiction to review the juvenile court's March 2016 order approving DCS's removal of O.E.

relevance.ACT-03: Establishes that an order approving removal and placement is separately appealable and must be challenged then, not later.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Arizona rule on appellate timeliness in juvenile cases — a fifteen-day window from each final order.

cases.case_name: Arizona Department of Economic Security v. Leonardo
cases.holding: The court of appeals held that the Interstate Compact on the Placement of Children applies to a court-ordered placement of dependent children with a noncustodial out-of-state parent, and vacated the portions of the orders directing placement without ICPC compliance.
cases.quote: it does place her within the category of persons to whom the ICPC applies, based on the language of the compact, its policy and purpose, and Regulation 3

relevance.ACT-04: Requires ICPC compliance — including an out-of-state home study — before a dependent child is placed with an out-of-state parent or relative.
relevance.OUT-03: Conditions out-of-state kinship permanency on the receiving state's ICPC approval.

cases.case_name: Titus S. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The court of appeals reversed the order terminating an out-of-state father's rights, holding the best-interests finding was an abuse of discretion where the current caregivers would not consent to adoption and no evidence suggested adoption was otherwise likely.
cases.quote: In these circumstances, where there is no evidentiary basis to suggest adoption is likely, we conclude the severe and permanent consequence of termination is unwarranted.

relevance.OUT-02: Limits reliance on prospective adoption as the benefit supporting a best-interests finding where adoption is not in fact realistic.
relevance.OUT-05: Supports refusing or dismissing a termination petition where severance would leave the child in legal limbo.

cases.case_name: Diana H. v. Rubin
cases.holding: The court of appeals vacated the order authorizing the agency to consent to immunizations, holding that a dependency adjudication does not extinguish a parent's residual right to direct her child's religious upbringing and that the State had not shown a compelling interest overriding her religious objection.
cases.quote: the state's responsibility to provide medical care for a dependent child is expressly "subject to" a body of parental rights and duties retained by the parent

relevance.INP-07: Confirms that a medical encounter and resulting agency custody do not transfer all parental medical decision authority to the State.
relevance.ACT-05: Defines the residual parental rights that survive a protective order or dependency disposition.
relevance.ACT-06: The controlling Arizona case on the agency's authority to authorize medical care for a child in its custody over parental objection.

cases.case_name: In re Timothy C.
cases.holding: The court of appeals held that a Child Protective Services caseworker who obtained a juvenile's confession was a state actor for due process purposes and that the State failed to overcome the presumption that the confession was involuntary.
cases.quote: We hold that the CPS caseworker was a state actor for purposes of a due process analysis.

relevance.INP-01: Establishes that the caseworker who receives and acts on a report is a state actor bound by constitutional limits.
relevance.INP-03: Governs CPS interviews that run parallel to or feed a criminal investigation.
relevance.INP-08: Applies to caseworker questioning of a minor outside the home, including in school and institutional settings.
relevance.INP-10: Constrains how an agency may escalate from screening to interrogation-style investigative interviews.
relevance.DEC-02: The controlling Arizona authority that constitutional protections attach to CPS investigative interviews.

cases.case_name: Lorenz v. State
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed dismissal of grandparents' civil suit against DCS, holding the child-welfare statutes, rules, and policies they invoked create no civil duty running to relatives who seek placement of a dependent child.
cases.quote: Because the cited authorities reveal an intent to protect and benefit dependent children, not potential foster or adoptive placements, we affirm the superior court's judgment.

relevance.INP-05: Establishes that a relative's request for involvement creates no enforceable civil duty on the agency.
relevance.DEC-01: Shows that an agency's decision not to act on a relative's information is not privately actionable.
relevance.DEC-06: Confirms agency discretion in front-end case handling is not constrained by a private duty to relatives.
relevance.ACT-04: The controlling Arizona case on whether relatives can sue over a denied kinship placement.
relevance.OUT-04: Limits the private enforcement remedies available where an agency's placement decisions shape a youth's path to permanency.
relevance.OUT-06: Marks the boundary of state-law tort liability where agency conduct is alleged to have harmed a child.
relevance.FAIL-04: Shows that Arizona's child-welfare statutes generally do not create a private right of action for agency failures.
relevance.FAIL-05: Distinguishes discretionary placement decisions from actionable discrimination or retaliation claims.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed and remanded, holding that due process requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights, while leaving any higher standard to state law.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

relevance.DEC-03: Supplies the federal due process floor that constrains how a state's abuse or neglect findings may be used to sever a family.
relevance.OUT-02: The federal constitutional minimum burden of proof for termination, which Arizona applies to the statutory ground.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court affirmed, holding that due process does not categorically require appointed counsel in every parental termination proceeding and leaving the question to case-by-case determination by the trial court subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.FAIL-01: The federal baseline on appointed counsel against which Arizona's broader statutory right and its effective-assistance standard operate.

cases.case_name: Haaland v. Brackeen
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court affirmed that Congress had constitutional authority to enact ICWA, reversed the anticommandeering holdings below, and vacated the equal protection and nondelegation rulings for want of standing, leaving ICWA's requirements and placement preferences operative in state proceedings.
cases.quote: we affirm the judgment of the Court of Appeals regarding Congress's constitutional authority to enact ICWA

relevance.INP-11: Settles that ICWA validly binds Arizona state courts once an Indian child is identified.
relevance.FAIL-03: Confirms that federal child-welfare mandates may lawfully be imposed on state agencies and courts.
relevance.FAIL-05: Leaves the equal protection challenge to ICWA's placement preferences unresolved on the merits for want of standing.

cases.case_name: Demaree v. Pederson
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: In an Arizona case, the Ninth Circuit reversed summary judgment based on qualified immunity and remanded, holding that on the plaintiffs' version of the facts the social workers lacked reasonable cause to believe the children faced articulable, imminent, serious physical injury or molestation and so violated clearly established rights by removing them without a court order.
cases.quote: The clearly established case law requires articulable, imminent, and serious physical injury or physical abuse to children to justify removing them from their parents' home without a judicial order.

relevance.INP-12: States the exact quantum of risk required before Arizona caseworkers may take emergency custody without judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: The controlling Arizona-arising articulation of the exigency standard for warrantless removal.
relevance.ACT-03: Confirms that placing children in foster care after an unjustified removal does not cure the constitutional violation.
relevance.FAIL-02: Holds the right against non-exigent warrantless removal clearly established, defeating qualified immunity.

cases.case_name: Kirkpatrick v. County of Washoe
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The en banc Ninth Circuit held a jury could find the warrantless seizure of a newborn unconstitutional because there was time to obtain a warrant, granted the individual caseworkers qualified immunity because that obligation was not clearly established at the time, and reversed and remanded the municipal-liability claim.
cases.quote: We hold that Kirkpatrick has raised a genuine dispute as to whether B.W. was in such imminent danger of serious bodily injury that no warrant was necessary.

relevance.INP-12: Establishes that exigency requires not only danger but insufficient time to obtain judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: Binding circuit authority in Arizona that a warrant is required for removal whenever there is time to get one.
relevance.FAIL-02: Provides the municipal-liability route where an agency maintains a policy of seizing children in non-exigent circumstances.

cases.case_name: Wallis ex rel. Wallis v. Spencer
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The Ninth Circuit reversed summary judgment for the city on the § 1983 claims, holding that absent risk of dissipating evidence or an urgent medical problem the state must notify parents and obtain judicial approval before subjecting children in protective custody to investigatory physical examinations, and that a jury must decide whether there was reasonable cause for the removal.
cases.quote: The right to family association includes the right of parents to make important medical decisions for their children

relevance.INP-03: Governs law enforcement's role in removing and examining children on the basis of a referral it has not corroborated.
relevance.INP-07: Requires parental notice and judicial approval before an investigatory medical or forensic examination of a child in custody.
relevance.INP-12: Confirms that protective custody does not by itself authorize intrusive examinations of the child.
relevance.DEC-04: Reasonable cause for emergency removal is a fact question where the underlying report is uncorroborated.
relevance.ACT-06: The leading circuit authority distinguishing urgent medical treatment from investigatory examinations of a child in state custody.
relevance.FAIL-02: Establishes municipal § 1983 liability for a policy of removing children on a non-existent court order.

cases.case_name: Calabretta v. Floyd
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that a social worker and a police officer who coerced entry into a home and strip-searched a child during a child-abuse investigation, without a warrant, consent, or exigency, violated clearly established Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
cases.quote: everyone knew that the government could not so enter houses, and White said that principle was well established, in the context of a child abuse investigation

relevance.INP-03: Holds that a police escort does not supply the authority a caseworker lacks to enter a home.
relevance.INP-06: Establishes that an uncorroborated tip does not create the exigency needed to enter a home without consent.
relevance.DEC-02: The controlling circuit rule that Fourth Amendment warrant, consent, or exigency requirements apply to CPS home investigations.
relevance.FAIL-02: Denies qualified immunity for warrantless investigative entry and search in a child-abuse case.

cases.case_name: Momox-Caselis v. Donohue
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the county and its officials in a suit over a foster child's death, holding the family failed to prove deliberate indifference under the special-relationship exception or to establish a Monell claim given the county's licensing and training policies.
cases.quote: The "special relationship" exception applies when there is a custodial relationship between the plaintiff and the State, such that the State assumes some responsibility for the plaintiff's safety and well-being.

relevance.ACT-03: Defines the constitutional duty the State assumes toward a child once it places the child in foster care.
relevance.ACT-06: Addresses medication and caregiving failures in a licensed foster home as a substantive due process question.
relevance.OUT-04: Frames the State's continuing custodial duty to youth who remain in its care.
relevance.OUT-06: The controlling circuit standard — deliberate indifference — for constitutional claims arising from a child's death in foster care.
relevance.FAIL-03: Shows that documented licensing and training compliance defeats a claim of systemic constitutional failure.
relevance.FAIL-04: Sets the demanding proof required to hold an agency liable for a child death under its supervision.
relevance.PMC-01: Illustrates how agency licensing and training records become the evidentiary core of systemic oversight claims.
relevance.PMC-04: Supplies the legal frame within which fatality reviews of deaths in care are litigated.

cases.case_name: Capp v. County of San Diego
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that a father plausibly alleged a First Amendment retaliation claim where a social worker threatened to initiate dependency proceedings because he questioned the allegations and criticized the county, and that the social worker was not entitled to qualified immunity on that claim.
cases.quote: We also conclude, however, that Plaintiffs plead a viable First Amendment retaliation claim, and that Defendants are not entitled to qualified immunity on this claim.

relevance.FAIL-05: The controlling circuit authority that a caseworker's retaliation against a parent for protected criticism is actionable under § 1983.

cases.case_name: Demetrius L. v. Joshlynn F.
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals and affirmed the juvenile court's best-interests finding, holding that a prospective adoption — including by a stepparent in a private severance action — is a benefit that can support a finding that termination is in the child's best interests, and that the court of appeals erred by overturning a finding supported by reasonable evidence.
cases.quote: a juvenile court may conclude that a proposed adoption benefits the child and supports a finding that severance is in the child's best interests

relevance.OUT-02: The Arizona Supreme Court's controlling statement that a prospective adoption is a cognizable benefit in the best-interests inquiry, in private as well as state-initiated severance actions.
relevance.FAIL-01: States the deferential standard of review — findings stand if reasonable evidence supports them — and holds that the court of appeals erred in reversing a supported best-interests finding.

cases.case_name: Mary Lou C. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the severance order, holding that the State's constitutionally grounded obligation to make a reasonable effort to preserve the family applies to the prior-severance ground of A.R.S. § 8-533(B)(10) as it does to other grounds, but affirming because the record supported an implicit finding that further rehabilitative services would have been futile.
cases.quote: The requirement that ADES make an effort to preserve the family is mandated on constitutional grounds

relevance.ACT-01: The leading post-Mary Ellen C. Arizona application of the rule that offered services must be genuine, holding the preservation duty is constitutionally rooted rather than merely statutory.
relevance.ACT-02: Extends the reasonable-efforts/appropriate-services requirement to a severance ground that does not name it, so a court-ordered service plan cannot be skipped by pleading around it.
relevance.DEC-06: Confirms the agency's service obligation attaches before any petition-based ground is proven, which is the legal premise of a services-without-petition track.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines the futility exception — the only basis on which the State may dispense with reunification services — against which a failed reunification is measured.

cases.case_name: Steven H. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and remanded, holding that 25 U.S.C. § 1912(e) requires qualified expert testimony addressing the likelihood of future serious harm to the Indian child, but that the testimony need not recite the statutory language or be expressed in any particular form.
cases.quote: ICWA requires qualified expert testimony that addresses the determination that the Indian child is at risk of future harm unless the child is removed from the parents' custody

relevance.INP-11: The Arizona Supreme Court's controlling construction of ICWA's qualified-expert-witness requirement — what the expert must actually address before an Indian child may be placed in foster care.

cases.case_name: Gila River Indian Community v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' 2016 opinion and affirmed the denial of the tribe's transfer motion, holding that 25 U.S.C. § 1911(b) governs transfer only of foster-care-placement and termination proceedings, that it neither applies to nor prohibits transfer of preadoptive and adoptive placements, and declining to rest on waiver.
cases.quote: We hold that § 1911(b) addresses transfer only of foster care placement and termination-of-parental-rights actions

relevance.INP-11: The Arizona Supreme Court's controlling statement of when § 1911(b) transfer to tribal court is available, superseding the 2016 court of appeals decision this brief previously relied on and rejecting its implied-waiver rationale.

cases.case_name: In Re the Appeal in Cochise County Juvenile Action No. 5666-J
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the juvenile court's dismissal of the dependency petition, holding that Santosky's clear-and-convincing standard is confined to termination and that dependency must be proved only by a preponderance of the evidence, which the State had not done.
cases.quote: the weighing of the private and public interests convinces us that the preponderance of the evidence standard is the proper standard of proof in dependency proceedings

relevance.INP-04: The Arizona Supreme Court source of the evidentiary threshold a referral must ultimately meet once a judge sends a family into the juvenile court.
relevance.DEC-03: Marks the constitutional line Santosky draws — a finding short of termination does not carry the clear-and-convincing burden, but the State must still prove abuse or neglect in court.
relevance.DEC-05: The controlling Arizona authority on the dependency burden of proof, which the later court of appeals decisions merely follow and expressly cite.

cases.case_name: Daniel Y. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals vacated the severance order and remanded for a new severance proceeding, holding that irreconcilable differences with two prior appointed lawyers did not, without advance warning or a finding of egregious conduct, waive or forfeit the parent's right to appointed counsel.
cases.quote: the failure to allow counsel to effectively participate in severance proceedings is reversible error

relevance.FAIL-01: The Arizona foundation for reversing a severance order on counsel grounds, and the case Donald W. and Tammy M. both build on — denial of effective participation of counsel is reversible without a showing of prejudice.

cases.case_name: Manuel M. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the termination order, holding that a parent who fails to appear admits only the factual allegations of the motion, that counsel retains the right to participate and contest whether those facts establish a statutory ground by clear and convincing evidence, and that the evidentiary errors below were harmless.
cases.quote: The parent does not thereby concede that those factual allegations sustain the quantum of evidence required to establish the legal grounds for terminating a parent's rights

relevance.FAIL-01: The leading pre-Brenda D. Arizona decision on non-appearance at a termination hearing — it fixes the limits of the constructive admission and preserves counsel's role, and so defines when a default-based severance is reversible.

cases.case_name: Denise R. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the termination order but restated the appellate standard of review, holding that review of a severance order, while deferential, must incorporate the juvenile court's clear-and-convincing burden and will affirm unless no reasonable factfinder could find the grounds clear and convincing.
cases.quote: we conclude our standard of review for orders terminating parental rights, while deferential, must reflect the requirement that grounds be proven by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the sufficiency-of-the-evidence standard an Arizona appellate court actually applies when asked to reverse a severance order, and the requirement that the reviewing court test the record against the clear-and-convincing burden.

cases.case_name: Marianne N. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated part of the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the termination order, holding that applying Rule 64(C)'s waiver-for-nonappearance provision at pretrial proceedings harmonizes with, and does not unconstitutionally conflict with, A.R.S. § 8-863(C).
cases.quote: We here hold that applying Rule 64(C) in pretrial proceedings does not conflict with § 8-863(C) in violation of the separation of powers required by the Arizona Constitution, article 3

relevance.FAIL-01: Forecloses the separation-of-powers attack on Rule 64(C) accelerated severances, narrowing the grounds on which a parent may obtain reversal after failing to appear at a pretrial or status conference.

cases.case_name: Antonio P. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the placement of the child with an aunt and uncle over a grandmother, holding that the A.R.S. § 8-514(B) order of placement is a preference rather than a mandate and that the juvenile court need only include it in its best-interests analysis.
cases.quote: The statute requires only that the court include placement preference in its analysis of what is in the child's best interest

relevance.ACT-04: The A.R.S. § 8-514(B) placement-preference framework that Jeff D. later applies and quotes — it establishes that the statutory kinship ranking is a factor the court must weigh, not an order it must follow.

cases.case_name: Trisha A. v. Department of Child Safety
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the severance order, holding that a parent moving under Rule 46(E) to set aside a severance judgment entered after a Rule 64(C) acceleration must show a meritorious defense, and that this requirement does not violate due process.
cases.quote: We hold that the meritorious defense requirement does not violate parents' due process rights

relevance.FAIL-01: The Arizona Supreme Court's controlling statement of what a parent must show to undo a severance judgment entered on nonappearance — good cause plus a meritorious defense — and the rejection of the due-process challenge to that burden.

cases.case_name: Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community v. Rogers
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the superior court's disclosure order, holding that a document is not a public record merely because a public officer possesses it and that it must bear some relation to the officer's official duties, and ordering the tribal check distribution list returned.
cases.quote: a public record must also have some relation to the official duties of the public officer that holds the record

relevance.INP-09: The foundational Arizona Supreme Court definition of what counts as a public record, which fixes the outer boundary of an oversight body's or requester's reach into agency files.
relevance.FAIL-06: Establishes the threshold question in every Arizona non-disclosure dispute — whether the document is a public record at all — which an agency must answer document by document rather than categorically.
relevance.PMC-05: The decision on which Griffis and ACLU v. DCS both expressly rest, supplying the three alternative definitions of 'public record' used in every Arizona transparency case.

cases.case_name: Carlson v. Pima County
cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court approved the court of appeals' decision and held that records a public officer is required to keep are presumed open to inspection, subject to the custodian's discretion to deny access where confidentiality, privacy, or the best interest of the state outweighs disclosure, with any such refusal subject to judicial scrutiny.
cases.quote: all records required to be kept under A.R.S. § 39-121.01(B), are presumed open to the public for inspection as public records

relevance.INP-09: The source of the presumption of openness that lets oversight bodies and the public demand agency records without first proving entitlement.
relevance.FAIL-06: Establishes that a custodian's refusal is discretionary, must rest on a weighed countervailing interest, and is reviewable by special action with fees and damages available for bad-faith denial.
relevance.PMC-02: Confirms that the records an agency is legally obliged to keep — the audit and expenditure trail — are precisely the records presumed disclosable.
relevance.PMC-05: The origin of the presumption of disclosure Griffis quotes, and the case that sets out the statutory remedy for wrongful denial under A.R.S. § 39-121.02.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the Due Process Clause imposed no affirmative constitutional duty on county caseworkers to protect a child from his father's violence, because the State had not restrained the child's liberty and so had no custodial special relationship with him.
cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

relevance.DEC-01: The controlling federal answer to the parent's or relative's claim that the agency's failure to act on a report is itself unconstitutional — knowledge of danger alone creates no duty.
relevance.ACT-03: Identifies the act that does create a constitutional duty: the State's affirmative restraint of the child's liberty, which is what a foster placement effects.
relevance.OUT-06: The federal baseline for every claim arising from a child's death or serious injury — liability turns on custody, not on the agency's awareness of the risk.
relevance.FAIL-04: Without this case Momox-Caselis is unintelligible; it explains why a documented history of referrals does not by itself make a child's death a constitutional violation.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that the 'reasonable efforts' requirement of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), is enforceable by the Secretary through the state-plan approval process but confers no privately enforceable right under § 1983 and creates no implied private cause of action.
cases.quote: We conclude that 42 U. S. C. § 671 (a)(15) neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf

relevance.ACT-02: Draws the line between Arizona's judicially enforceable state-law diligent-effort requirement and the federal Title IV-E 'reasonable efforts' condition, which a parent cannot sue on.
relevance.OUT-01: Explains why a failed reunification cannot be litigated as a federal statutory violation even where the agency's efforts fell short of the IV-E plan.
relevance.FAIL-03: Real, controlling authority for this node: federal child-welfare performance conditions are enforced administratively by HHS through funding, not by private suit.
relevance.FAIL-04: Forecloses the § 1983 route for systemic IV-E service failures, leaving constitutional claims and state law as the only private remedies.

cases.case_name: Camreta v. Greene
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held it could review a lower-court constitutional ruling at the behest of officials who won on qualified immunity, but, finding the case moot because the child had grown up and moved away, vacated the Ninth Circuit's Fourth Amendment holding on the in-school interview and remanded.
cases.quote: Mootness has frustrated his ability to challenge the Court of Appeals' ruling that he must obtain a warrant before interviewing a suspected child abuse victim at school

relevance.INP-08: Corrects the record for this node: the Ninth Circuit's holding in Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011 (9th Cir. 2009), that CPS must obtain a warrant before interviewing a suspected victim at school was VACATED and is not law, so no binding circuit rule governs CPS school interviews in Arizona.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed and remanded, holding that 'domicile' under ICWA is a uniform federal standard, that twins born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were themselves domiciled on the reservation, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a) notwithstanding the mother's voluntary surrender.
cases.quote: Tribal jurisdiction under § 1911(a) was not meant to be defeated by the actions of individual members of the tribe

relevance.INP-11: The controlling Supreme Court decision on how ICWA actually operates — it fixes exclusive tribal jurisdiction by federal-law domicile and forecloses parental workarounds, the threshold question in any Arizona case involving an Indian child.

cases.case_name: Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed and remanded, holding that ICWA § 1912(f) does not apply where the parent never had custody of the child, that § 1912(d)'s remedial-services requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family, and that § 1915(a)'s placement preferences do not apply when no preferred party has sought to adopt.
cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights

relevance.INP-11: The second controlling Supreme Court merits decision on ICWA's operation, marking the limits of §§ 1912(d), 1912(f) and 1915(a) once a case is identified as involving an Indian child.

cases.case_name: Stanley v. Illinois
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed and remanded, holding that an unwed father was denied due process and equal protection when Illinois declared his children dependent and removed them on a presumption of unfitness without any hearing on his actual fitness as a parent.
cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody

relevance.INP-04: The federal constitutional floor when a court opens a dependency inquiry against a parent — presumed unfitness cannot substitute for an individualized hearing.
relevance.DEC-05: A majority-opinion source for the parental liberty interest at the moment the State files to take a child, supplying the authority this brief correctly declined to draw from the Troxel plurality.

cases.case_name: Tamas v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The Ninth Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that foster children hold a clearly established Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in safe placement and social-worker protection once they become wards of the state, and that the district court had applied an erroneous deliberate-indifference standard to each official's liability.
cases.quote: The Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process clause protects a foster child's liberty interest in social worker supervision and protection from harm inflicted by a foster parent

relevance.ACT-03: The affirmative circuit statement of what the State owes a child once it places her in foster care — supervision and protection, not merely the absence of state-inflicted harm.
relevance.OUT-06: The better affirmative authority for a claim arising from abuse or death in care, cited inside Momox-Caselis but stated here as the governing right.
relevance.FAIL-04: Establishes that each official's liability is assessed individually on what she knew and inferred, which is the framework a fatality or serious-injury claim must satisfy.

cases.case_name: Mabe v. San Bernardino County
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that a triable issue existed as to whether the social worker had reasonable cause to believe the child faced imminent danger of serious bodily injury justifying warrantless entry and seizure, and that probable cause supporting a warrant does not itself establish the exigency a warrantless removal requires.
cases.quote: a showing of probable cause does not satisfy the conclusion that MD was in imminent danger of serious physical injury sufficient to justify a warrantless removal

relevance.INP-12: The source authority for the imminent-danger standard Arizona caseworkers must satisfy before taking protective custody without a court order, cited here directly rather than second-hand.
relevance.DEC-04: Draws the operative distinction at the removal decision — enough to get a warrant is not enough to act without one.
relevance.FAIL-02: Establishes that a caseworker's delay in acting is itself evidence that no exigency existed, defeating summary judgment on an unlawful-removal claim.

cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The Ninth Circuit reversed the grant of qualified immunity to the social worker and reversed the denial of the parents' partial summary judgment motion, holding it was clearly established that children may be removed without a warrant only in exigent circumstances and that no reasonable social worker could have found exigency on these facts of medical neglect.
cases.quote: it was clearly established that warrantless removal of children is permissible only in cases of exigency

relevance.INP-12: Confirms that neglect findings, even serious ones, do not supply the exigency that alone permits protective custody without judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: The companion source authority to Mabe for the reasonable-cause/imminent-danger test governing the emergency removal decision in the Ninth Circuit.
relevance.FAIL-02: Holds the right clearly established and strips qualified immunity where the agency's own ten-day response classification shows it perceived no emergency.

notes: METHOD: every case below was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read. All 42 quotes were mechanically verified to be exact substrings of the retrieved opinion text (whitespace and curly-quote/dash characters normalized) and were confirmed by line/offset position to fall within the majority (or per curiam / en banc majority) opinion, not a syllabus, headnote, concurrence or dissent. For the Ninth Circuit opinions the court-staff 'SUMMARY' block was excluded before quoting; for Momox-Caselis and Capp the quote was confirmed present in the opinion body and absent from the summary.
NO UNPUBLISHED DECISIONS WERE USED. Every Arizona case listed is a published opinion of the Arizona Supreme Court or the Arizona Court of Appeals.

EXISTING key_cases IN THE AZ FILES ARE NOISE. All 43 AZ node files carry the same eight keyword-matched titles. 'In the matter of CHALMERS', 'In re Sponsel', 'In the Matter of WITT', 'In re: RIGGINS', 'IN RE THE MARRIAGE OF QUIJADA/DOMINGUEZ' and the 'Decision Order' entries for DANIEL R RAYNAK and DONALD H SMITH are attorney-discipline and domestic-relations matters with no bearing on child welfare; none was retained. Only three of the eight titles corresponded to real, on-point Arizona decisions -- ACLU of Arizona v. Arizona DCS, In re Termination of Parental Rights as to B.W., and In re Termination of Parental Rights as to M.N. -- and each of those three was independently retrieved, read and verified here.

CITATION FORM CAVEAT FOR LAWYERS: where the CourtListener cluster carried no reporter citation, slip form was used per instruction. That affects In re Termination of Parental Rights as to B.W., Jessie D. v. DCS, Timothy B. v. DCS, Brionna J. v. DCS and Silverman v. ADES. Several of these ARE in fact reported -- Brionna J. itself cites 'Jessie D. v. Dep't of Child Safety, 251 Ariz. 574 (2021)' and 'Timothy B., 252 Ariz. at 480', and Brionna J. vacated an opinion reported at 253 Ariz. 271 (App. 2022). Confirm the parallel Arizona Reports cite before filing anything.

Alma S. (425 P.3d 1089), Brenda D. (410 P.3d 419), In re Guardianship of C.M. (549 P.3d 214), In re Guardianship of A.K. (557 P.3d 770), Titus S. (418 P.3d 1138) and In re M.N. (563 P.3d 136) show only a Pacific Reporter cite in the cluster; the parallel Arizona Reports cites exist (e.g., Alma S. is 245 Ariz. 146) and should be added when filing.

Wallis ex rel. Wallis v. Spencer: the cluster date_filed is 1999-09-14 but the operative, published opinion is the amended one reported at 202 F.3d 1126 (9th Cir. 2000). date_decided/year here follow the cluster; cite the 2000 amended opinion.

Demaree v. Pederson: 887 F.3d 870 is the amended per curiam issued with the order denying rehearing; it supersedes 880 F.3d 1066. The quote used is from the PER CURIAM portion, not Judge N.R. Smith's separate opinion or Judge Zouhary's partial dissent.

TROXEL v. GRANVILLE WAS RETRIEVED AND DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED. Justice O'Connor's lead opinion is a plurality, not a majority, so quoting it would violate the majority-opinion rule. Santosky v. Kramer supplies the majority statement of the parental liberty interest and the clear-and-convincing floor. Arizona courts (e.g., Jessie D.) nonetheless cite Troxel, 530 U.S. at 65, routinely.

CIRCUIT CASES ARISING OUTSIDE ARIZONA. Keates v. Koile and Demaree v. Pederson are the two Ninth Circuit removal cases that arose out of Arizona CPS/DCS conduct. Kirkpatrick (Nevada), Momox-Caselis (Nevada), Wallis (California), Calabretta (California) and Capp (California) arose elsewhere but are binding Ninth Circuit precedent in Arizona; that is disclosed rather than hidden. The same is true of the three circuit cases added in this pass: Tamas (Washington), Mabe (California) and Rogers v. County of San Joaquin (California).

MICHAEL J. CAVEAT. The often-quoted passage that the State's reasonable-efforts duty 'has a constitutional basis' appears in Justice Feldman's DISSENT in Michael J., quoting Mary Ellen C. The quote used here is from the majority. Cite Mary Ellen C. v. ADES, 193 Ariz. 185 (App. 1999), for the constitutional reasonable-efforts holding.

VALERIE M. CAVEAT. Valerie M. arose from a jury trial; Arizona abolished jury trials in termination proceedings effective January 1, 2007 (2003 Ariz. Sess. Laws, ch. 6, sec. 10 (2d Spec. Sess.)). Its jury-instruction procedural discussion is historical; its ICWA burden-of-proof holding stands.

SILVERMAN v. ADES CAVEAT -- READ BEFORE CITING. Silverman construes A.R.S. sec. 46-460, the ADULT Protective Services confidentiality statute for vulnerable adults, not A.R.S. sec. 8-807, the child-welfare records statute. It is included at INP-09, FAIL-06 and the PMC nodes only for the Arizona Supreme Court's construction of a protective-services confidentiality statute's 'bona fide research' exception. Do NOT cite it as a child-welfare records case. ACLU of Arizona v. Arizona DCS, 240 Ariz. 142 (App. 2016), is the on-point child-welfare records authority.

NO ARIZONA AUTHORITY FOUND -- EXTENDED FOSTER CARE (OUT-04). Targeted searches of both Arizona courts for extended foster care, voluntary young-adult program, and juvenile court jurisdiction past age eighteen returned nothing on point. OUT-04 is therefore populated with the closest Arizona and Ninth Circuit authority on permanency and on the State's continuing custodial duty. The governing law for this node is statutory: the Chafee Foster Care Independence Act (Pub. L. 106-169), the Fostering Connections Act (Pub. L. 110-351), and A.R.S. sec. 8-521.02.

NO ARIZONA AUTHORITY FOUND -- CHILDREN MISSING FROM FOSTER CARE. No Arizona appellate decision was located addressing children who go missing from agency care or the agency's locate-and-report duties under 42 U.S.C. sec. 671(a)(35).

NO ARIZONA AUTHORITY FOUND -- CENTRAL REGISTRY DUE PROCESS. Searches for Arizona decisions on the A.R.S. sec. 8-804 / 8-804.02 central registry and the due-process hearing rights attaching to a substantiated finding returned nothing published and on point. DEC-03 is therefore built on the dependency burden-of-proof cases, reporter-immunity law, and the Santosky federal floor. A practitioner should confirm current registry-appeal procedure directly under A.R.S. sec. 8-811 and the tiered-registry statute rather than relying on case law.

NO ARIZONA AUTHORITY FOUND -- SCREEN-OUT (DEC-01) AND DIFFERENTIAL RESPONSE (DEC-06). Arizona has no published decision adjudicating an intake screen-out, an unfounded closure, or a differential/alternative response track. Those nodes carry the nearest real Arizona authority: reporter immunity for reports that go nowhere (Ramsey; Ludwig), the absence of a private civil duty arising from agency front-end decisions (Lorenz), and the reasonable-efforts/services duty (Mary Ellen C.; Mary Lou C.; Shawanee S.). DEC-01 now also carries the controlling federal standard, DeShaney v. Winnebago County, 489 U.S. 189 (1989), which is the answer a court will give to any claim that an agency's failure to act on a report was itself unconstitutional.

CORRECTED -- CPS SCHOOL INTERVIEWS (INP-08). The prior note directing a practitioner to research Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011 (9th Cir. 2009), was affirmatively misleading and is withdrawn. Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011), was retrieved and read in this session: the Supreme Court VACATED the Ninth Circuit's Fourth Amendment holding as moot. There is therefore NO binding circuit rule requiring a warrant before a CPS interview of a suspected victim at school in Arizona, and no published Arizona decision on the question either. INP-08 carries Camreta (to record the vacatur), L.A.R. v. Ludwig (reporter immunity for school professionals) and In re Timothy C. (the caseworker is a state actor when questioning a minor).

NO CASE LAW EXISTS -- PMC-01 THROUGH PMC-06. Federal oversight mechanisms (CFSR under 45 C.F.R. pt. 1355; HHS OIG and Single Audit Act reviews; Citizen Review Panels under 42 U.S.C. sec. 5106a(c); the Protect Our Kids Act commission, Pub. L. 112-275) are administered administratively and generate essentially no litigated appellate authority in Arizona. These six nodes are therefore populated with the only Arizona decisions that actually adjudicate access to and oversight of protective-services records and data (ACLU of Arizona v. Arizona DCS; Griffis v. Pinal County; Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Cmty. v. Rogers; Carlson v. Pima County; Silverman v. ADES) plus, at PMC-01/PMC-04, the Ninth Circuit's systemic-failure standard (Momox-Caselis). These are the authorities that make oversight operational in Arizona; they are not themselves oversight-statute cases, and the entries say so.

FAIL-03 (federal compliance failure) no longer reports 'no authority.' Suter v. Artist M., 503 U.S. 347 (1992), was retrieved and read in this session and is the controlling federal holding for this node: the Title IV-E 'reasonable efforts' condition is enforced by the Secretary through state-plan approval and funding, not by private suit. FAIL-03 now carries Suter together with Brackeen (federal mandates validly bind state agencies), Momox-Caselis (what systemic failure must be proved), and ACLU v. DCS (access to the performance data).

Added Demetrius L. v. Joshlynn F., 239 Ariz. 1 (2016) for OUT-02 (and relevant to FAIL-01): the Arizona Supreme Court's controlling statement that a prospective adoption is a benefit supporting a best-interests finding, and of the deferential standard of review that Alma S., Jessie D. and Brionna J. all build on.

Added Mary Lou C. v. Ariz. Dep't of Econ. NODE_MAP CURATION RULE AND ONE DEVIATION. Where adding leading authority would have pushed a node past the six-case guideline, node_map lists the six most authoritative entries (Arizona Supreme Court first, then the U.S. Supreme Court or Ninth Circuit where the node turns on a federal standard, then the Arizona Court of Appeals); the fuller set of nodes each case serves remains recorded in that case's relevance object. Cases curated out of a node_map list but still declaring relevance there: Alma S., Demetrius L. and Tammy M. at FAIL-01; Titus S. at OUT-02; Demaree at ACT-03; Navajo Nation and In re Guardianship of A.K. at INP-11; Adoptive Couple at ACT-04; Santosky at DEC-03 (retained) . ONE NODE EXCEEDS THE GUIDELINE: FAIL-01 carries nine authorities, because Arizona's law on reversing a severance order is split across six genuinely distinct doctrines -- scope of appellate review (Brionna J.), failure to appear (Brenda D.; Manuel M.), Rule 64(C) waiver at pretrial (Marianne N.), Rule 46(E) set-aside and meritorious defense (Trisha A.), sufficiency review under the clear-and-convincing burden (Denise R.), and the right to and effectiveness of counsel (Daniel Y.; Donald W.; Lassiter). No single case covers more than one of these, and cutting to six would have silently dropped a ground a parent's lawyer must know about.
